text: What this is about A small rectangular battery is labeled 9 V. This figure is a voltage . It does not say how much energy the battery contains, but how much energy each unit of charge gives up as it passes from one terminal to the other 9 joules per coulomb. Charge is the property of certain particles of exerting and feeling electric forces. The joule is the unit of energy, the coulomb the unit of charge. The question of this chapter is Why is voltage always a difference between two points, and what does it do to a charge? The answer leads through two concepts. An electric field determines, for every location, what force acts on a charge there. The potential determines, for every location, how much energy per coulomb a charge has there relative to a freely chosen zero point, the reference point . How to work with this chapter. text: The discipline of electrical engineering is the engineering science that moves electric charges in a controlled way in order to transmit energy and process information. A power plant, a motor, a wireless network and a processor all rest on the same process forces set charges in motion. Physics describes nature with measurable quantities and looks for the laws connecting them. The engineering sciences apply these laws, for example in components, circuits connections of components and power plants. All materials consist of atoms. An atom has a tiny nucleus of protons and neutrons , around which electrons move Fig. 1 abb 1 . Protons carry a positive charge, electrons a negative charge of exactly the same size, neutrons none. An atom contains as many protons as electrons; seen from outside, their charges cancel, and it is neutral . If it loses an electron, a positive charge is left over. An atom with a surplus charge is called an ion . Protons sit firmly in the nucleus and are 1836 times heavier than electrons, whereas outer electrons can be detached. That is why electrons are what moves in nearly all processes of electrical engineering. Diagram of an atom with three protons and three neutrons. Left, neutral three positive and three negative charges add up to zero. Right, one electron is missing the ion carries the charge . text: This stage settles the first question What is charge, how does a charged body come about, and what is conserved in the process? The idea. Frictional electricity, lightning as the discharge of separated charges through the air, and magnetism cannot be explained by mechanics. If a glass rod is rubbed with a silk cloth and a hard rubber rod with fur, the two rods attract each other, while two hard rubber rods repel Fig. 3 abb 3 . Rubbing creates nothing new; electrons change bodies. Different materials bind their outer electrons with different strength. At the points of contact, electrons pass to the material that binds them more strongly, and rubbing creates many such points. A body with an electron deficit is positively charged, one with an electron excess negatively. Top rubbing separates charge. Electrons pass from the glass to the silk and from the fur to the rubber. Bottom oppositely charged rods attract, like charged rods repel. A body with protons and electrons carries the charge The elementary charge is the smallest charge occurring freely. An electron carries , a proton . In a closed system, the sum of all charges stays constant conservation of charge . ⁠ How to read it Charge occurs only in multiples of ; one coulomb is elementary charges. Rubbed rods carry around 10 nC. Validity These steps are noticeable only for individual particles; even 1 nC is six billion electrons. In circuits, charge is therefore treated as a continuous quantity. Two bodies together carry . If an electron passes from 1 to 2, decreases by one and increases by one; the bracket stays the same. The charges “generated” by rubbing always add up to zero. The names are older than the electron. In 1733 DuFay distinguished vitreous and resinous electricity; around 1750 Franklin called one positive and the other negative. The Greek word for amber, elektron , gave the field its name. Conductors and insulators. In a conductor such as metal, at least one electron per atom can wander through the entire body. In an insulator such as glass or rubber, the electrons stay with their atoms. That is why charge on an insulator stays where it was produced, whereas on metal it spreads immediately. Example. Sphere A nC lacks electrons. A plastic sphere of 1 g contains around electrons, so only one in is missing. Limiting case For , . A neutral body does not contain little charge; it contains equal amounts of both signs. Because the signs were assigned before electrons were known. Franklin called rubbed glass positive; only much later did it turn out that glass loses electrons in the process. The convention stayed, so the electron carries negative charge. There is nothing special about this physically. After rubbing, a glass rod carries nC. How many electrons has it given up? What charge does the cloth carry if both were neutral beforehand? Two identical metal spheres carry nC and nC. They touch and are separated. What charge does each carry? How many electrons have moved across, and in which direction? a electrons. The cloth has taken them up and carries nC. b The total charge nC is conserved and divides evenly between identical spheres nC each. The negative sphere therefore gives electrons to the positive one.

In metal, the free electrons move until no force acts on them any more. This displacement is called electrostatic induction . A field line is a curve whose tangent at each point has the direction of ; the density of the lines shows the strength of the field. The following hold Field lines begin on positive charges sources and end on negative ones sinks , never in empty space. For a single charge, the other end runs off to infinity. Field lines do not cross. They are perpendicular to the surface of a conductor. Inside a conductor, . A charge free cavity enclosed by the conductor is field free shielding . ⁠ How to read it Rules 1 and 2 hold in empty space; rules 3 and 4 say what metal changes about the field. Nothing flows at sources and sinks; the words mean the beginning and end of the lines. Bottom right metal tube in cross section between two plates. Electrons collect on the left, positive charges remain on the right, inside . ⁠ Rule 2. At an intersection, would have two directions, but the force on a test charge is unique. ⁠ Rule 4, metal. If there were a field in the metal, the free electrons would keep moving. Rest is reached only when the displaced charges exactly cancel the external field inside. Excess charges sit on the surface. ⁠ Rule 3. A field component along the surface would push the electrons along it. At rest, only the perpendicular component remains. ⁠ Rule 4, cavity. The external field ends on the induced charges of the outer side. With no charge in the cavity, a line there would have to run from wall to wall. In the pair of plates, the charge sits on the inner sides of the plates, and the lines run parallel and equally dense from A to B. Equal density means that is the same everywhere; the field is uniform . This holds as long as is small compared with the plate width; only at the edge does a weaker fringing field bulge outward. The tube in Fig. 6 abb 6 shows rules 3 and 4; at its apex the field is around twice as strong as without the tube. A closed metal shell protects its interior, which is why you are safe in a car during a thunderstorm. ⁠ Check Rule 1 fits Coulomb's law. From a charge, lines run evenly in all directions and pierce a sphere of area . The density falls with , hence also the factor in . Conversely, shielding is perfect only for an exponent of exactly 2. text: Everything so far held for charges at rest. This stage shows what changes when charges move and magnetic fields change, and where path independence ends. The idea. For a long time, electricity and magnetism were regarded as separate fields. In 1820 Ørsted saw a compass needle deflect next to a current carrying wire moving charge produces a magnetic field . In 1831 Faraday reversed the idea a magnet that he moved in a coil , a wire wound into turns, produced a voltage at its ends. This is called induction . In 1864 Maxwell combined everything into electromagnetism . The mechanism of induction is a new field a changing magnetic field produces an electric field with closed lines, a curl field . On one round trip in it, a charge gains energy, and that ends the statement 6.2 arbeit im feld.html gl 6 2 . Left cross section of a wire; the current flows into the page. The magnetic field runs in circles around the wire, and compass needles align their red tips with it. Right a moving bar magnet changes the magnetic flux through the coil. As long as it moves, the meter shows the voltage . The direction of the magnetic field is given by the right hand rule the thumb points in the conventional current direction, the fingers in the direction of the field. The conventional current direction runs from plus to minus; the electrons in the wire move the opposite way Part 2 /wissen/en/elektrotechnik/1 semester/grundlagen der elektrotechnik/strom widerstand und kirchhoff/strom widerstand und kirchhoff.html . If the magnetic flux through a coil with turns changes, the following voltage arises between its ends ⁠ How to read it The magnetic flux measures how much magnetic field passes through the coil area, weber . Small coils carry microwebers to milliwebers. Only the change counts, not the flux itself. The law is a measurement result along one turn, the curl field supplies the voltage ; the turns are in series and their voltages add. The lowercase letter stands for a time dependent voltage. The minus sign says that a current driven by this voltage opposes the change in flux. Validity All turns must enclose the same flux. Faraday also showed induction without a magnet he wound two coils onto a ring and connected a battery to one and a galvanometer an early current meter to the other. It deflected only when switching on and off, because only then does the flux change. Maxwell's equations in words. The equations themselves need more mathematics, but their content fits into four sentences. The flux density here is the measure of the density of the field lines. Gauss's law for electric fields Charges are sources and sinks of the electric flux density. Gauss's law for magnetism The magnetic flux density has no sources; its lines are closed. Law of induction Changes of the magnetic flux in time lead to an electric curl field. Ampère's law Currents and changes of the electric field in time lead to a magnetic curl field. Example. The magnet in Fig. 12 abb 12 changes the flux through the coil with uniformly by 0.2 mWb in 25 ms. The voltage is then constant V. During this time, the loop integral of around the flux is not zero, and the voltage between two points depends on which side of the flux the path runs. ⁠ Limiting cases For constant flux, ; a magnet at rest produces no voltage. In most circuits, the changing fluxes sit almost entirely in coils. Between the components the field stays practically curl free, which is why potentials and voltages remain the tool there. The potential of a location is the work per charge up to the reference point. In a curl field, that depends on the path. Two paths give two values, and the location would have no unique potential. A coil with 200 turns encloses a flux that increases uniformly by 0.5 mWb in 10 ms. a How large is the magnitude of the induced voltage? b The flux then stays constant. What voltage is present now? a V. b Zero, because .

That depends on three things how densely the charge sits, how fast it moves and how large the cross section is. So . When does current flow continuously? Two conditions must be met. First, the circuit needs a source, such as a battery or a power supply. It supplies energy, not charge the charge carriers are already in the conductor; the source only drives them around the circuit. Second, the circuit must be closed, that is, a path that returns to itself. Otherwise charge piles up at a gap, its field cancels the driving field, and the current ends. The field, by contrast, spreads along the wire as an electromagnetic wave when the switch closes, in cables at around m/s. The electrons are already everywhere in the wire. text: From now on, what counts is no longer what happens inside the component, but what can be measured at its terminals. That requires a term for the component and an agreement about signs. The idea. For calculating, it is enough to know how a component responds to voltage with current. The inside may be unknown. Signs are fixed beforehand with arrows, because the true directions are often not known before the calculation. The result then says whether reality follows the arrow. A two terminal element is a component that can be fully described by the current and voltage between its two terminals. In the steady state time independent , that is its characteristic curve . A black box is a system whose outward behavior is known but whose construction is unknown or unimportant. A network is an interconnection of two terminal elements. If the characteristic curve is a straight line through the origin, ⁠ How to read it Such a linear two terminal element is the ohmic resistor Fig. 4 das ohmsche gesetz aus feld und stoen.html abb 4 right, each straight line one value . Batteries and voltage sources also belong to the building blocks of linear networks, but their characteristic curve does not pass through the origin Part 5 /wissen/en/elektrotechnik/1 semester/grundlagen der elektrotechnik/quellen und ersatzquellen/quellen und ersatzquellen.html . For a nonlinear two terminal element such as the incandescent lamp Fig. 5 reale widerstande werte und temperatur.html abb 5 right , depends on the operating point, and 5.1 gl 5 1 does not hold there. The voltage arrow points from 1 to 2 and means Part 1 /wissen/en/elektrotechnik/1 semester/grundlagen der elektrotechnik/ladung feld und potenzial/ladung feld und potenzial.html . The current arrow counts positive charge in the direction of the arrow. In the passive sign convention PSC, load convention , the voltage and current arrows at a two terminal element point in the same direction; in the active sign convention ASC, generator convention , they point in opposite directions. For a resistor, ⁠ How to read it Both conventions are only agreements. The direction of both arrows can be chosen freely; that changes signs, never the physics. The usual choice is the PSC at a load and the ASC at a source, because then all numbers are positive in normal operation Fig. 6 abb 6 left . Why this fits In a load, positive charge runs from high to low potential and gives up energy; current and voltage have the same direction. In a source, it is lifted from low to high potential; current and voltage have opposite directions. In the PSC, therefore means that energy is absorbed; in the ASC, it means that energy is delivered. text: The first kind of equation What does the conservation of charge demand at a node? The idea. A node is a piece of wire. If more flows in than out, charge collects on it and its potential rises. This lowers the voltage across the incoming resistors and raises it across the outgoing ones. The inflow falls and the outflow rises until both are equal. This self regulation takes place in nanoseconds. It is the mechanism behind the rule the node settles at exactly the potential at which nothing is left stuck. The sum of all currents flowing into a node is zero at every instant. Equivalently, the sum of the incoming currents equals the sum of the outgoing currents For a network with nodes, of these equations are independent. ⁠ How to read it The arrows can be chosen freely. If all point toward the node, at least one of the currents must be negative, or all are zero. With mixed arrows, incoming ones count as positive and outgoing ones as negative. Validity The node must not store any appreciable charge. That holds as long as the currents change slowly compared with the equalization time. The derivation gives a number for this. text: What this is about Two metal plates with an insulator between them this component is called a capacitor . If you connect it to a battery, current flows in the leads even though the plates do not touch. The current grows weaker and stops by itself. If you disconnect the battery, the voltage remains, and the component can drive current on its own. The question of this chapter is How can current flow into an insulator, why does it end by itself, and where is the energy afterward? Each plate is an electrode ; the insulator between them is called the dielectric . The quantity that characterizes the component is the capacitance it says how much charge sits on the plates per volt. The basic form is two flat plates, the parallel plate capacitor . text: The plates do not touch. Nevertheless, a meter in the lead shows current. This stage clarifies which charge moves where. The idea. The uncharged pair of plates is connected to the battery by wires Fig. 1 abb 1 . At the first moment both plates are at the same potential, but the battery terminals are 9 V apart. The potential drop therefore lies along the wires. There is a field there, and it pushes the free electrons in the metal. In the wire at plate A they run away from the plate to the plus terminal, in the wire at plate B from the minus terminal onto the plate. A loses electrons and becomes positive, B gains electrons and becomes negative. No electron crosses the gap every electron that arrives on B comes from the wire before it, not from A. With every displaced charge, the field between the plates grows and with it the voltage. The plates approach the potential of their terminals, the drop along the wires shrinks, the current decreases. At 9 V between the plates, each plate is at the potential of its terminal. No drop remains along the wires, no force acts on the electrons any more, and the current ends. Left the pair of plates during charging. Electrons run from plate A to the plus terminal, and just as many from the minus terminal onto plate B. The current counts in the direction of positive charge, that is, against the electrons, and is the same in both leads. No charge runs through the insulator; the field is there. Right the circuit symbol with reference arrows. A capacitor consists of two electrodes separated by a dielectric. Its charge is the charge of the positive electrode; the other carries . text: How much charge does a given voltage hold on the plates? The answer is a single number for each component. The idea. If you double the charge on both plates, each charge contributes its field twice. By the superposition from Part 1 /wissen/en/elektrotechnik/1 semester/grundlagen der elektrotechnik/ladung feld und potenzial/ladung feld und potenzial.html , the field doubles at every location, and its shape stays the same Fig. 2 abb 2 left . The voltage is the integral of the field from plate to plate, so it doubles too. and are therefore proportional. Their ratio does not depend on how much charge happens to be there, but only on shape, separation and material. The capacitance of a capacitor is the ratio of charge to voltage ⁠ How to read it is the charge of the positive plate in C coulombs , the voltage between the plates in V, the capacitance in F. At 1 F, one volt holds one coulomb. That is a great deal. Usual values are in the fF, pF, nF and µF ranges; electrolytic capacitors reach into the mF range. Do not confuse the symbols italic is the capacitance, upright C is the coulomb. Validity 2.1 gl 2 1 assumes that the material between the plates does not change with the field. text: Several capacitors can be treated like one. The only question is which quantity the circuit makes the same for all of them. The idea. ⁠ Parallel All upper plates hang on one wire, all lower plates on another. A wire without current has the same potential everywhere, so the same voltage is across all the capacitors. The circuit acts like an enlarged plate, and the charges add. Series The lower plate of and the upper plate of , together with their connecting wire, form an island a piece of conductor reached only through insulators Fig. 7 abb 7 . Charge can neither get in nor out there. If the island was uncharged, its sum stays zero if the upper plate with attracts on the island, the missing counterpart must go as onto the next plate. So all carry the same charge, and the voltages add. The circuit acts like an enlarged separation. and at 9 V. Parallel the same voltage; the charges add up to 1350 µC. text: Before an error can be calculated, it must be clear what a meter is electrically a component with two terminals and a resistance between them. The idea. In a pointer instrument, a rotatable coil of thin wire sits between the poles of a permanent magnet Fig. 1 abb 1 . When current flows, the magnetic field exerts a force on the moving electrons in the wire, and the coil turns against a spiral spring. The torque grows with the current, the counterforce of the spring with the angle. That is why the deflection is proportional to the current. Two things cannot be avoided without current there is no deflection, and with current a voltage drops across the wire. A digital multimeter a device with a numeric display converts the voltage across an internal resistor into a number. There, too, current flows through a resistor. Left, the meter movement the coil turns in the magnetic field against a spring not drawn . Right, the equivalent circuits ideal instrument plus internal resistance, in series or in parallel. The measuring range extends up to the full scale value , the largest value that can be displayed for a pointer, full scale deflection . The internal resistance is the resistance between the terminals. An ammeter is connected in series. Ideally , in practice about . A voltmeter is connected in parallel. Ideally , in practice about . ⁠ How to read it Current is charge passing through a cross section. That is why you open the circuit and send the entire current through the ammeter. text: Some networks contain no groups. Symmetry then supplies nodes of equal potential, and connecting them creates groups. The idea. If two nodes are at the same potential, the voltage between them is zero. A wire between them therefore carries no current, and nothing changes if you add it. Conversely, you may cut a current free branch. Symmetry reveals which nodes these are, without any calculation. For a network of resistors with the terminals A and B If mirroring or rotating maps the network onto itself while A and B stay in place, nodes that coincide have the same potential. You may connect them. A resistor between them carries no current. If mirroring maps the network onto itself while A and B swap places, every point on the mirror axis is at the mean value . You may connect all of them and calculate only one side, the half circuit ⁠ How to read it is the resistance between A and the axis connected into one node. A resistor crossing the axis splits into two half resistors, and its center lies on the axis. A resistor along the axis has both ends at the same potential and carries no current. Validity The symmetry must also cover the values. A single deviating resistor destroys it. text: What has been missing so far is whatever drives the current. This stage introduces the two basic building blocks that bring energy into a network. The idea. A source holds a single quantity fixed. The connected network determines the other. An ideal voltage source holds the potential difference between its terminals. The load decides what current flows. An ideal current source holds the current in its branch. The load likewise decides what voltage arises. Both are models. They cannot be built, but a regulated power supply or a transistor circuit Part 10 /wissen/en/elektrotechnik/1 semester/grundlagen der elektrotechnik/der bipolartransistor/der bipolartransistor.html comes close to them within a limited range. Left, the ideal voltage source in the diagram a horizontal line, the voltage does not depend on the current. Right, the ideal current source a vertical line, the current does not depend on the voltage. The stroke in the circuit symbol shows the behavior at the value zero drawn along the line, the line is closed; drawn across it, the line is interrupted. For the ideal voltage source and the ideal current source, ⁠ How to read it is the source voltage in V, from millivolts to kilovolts, here 9 V. is the source current in A, from microamperes to amperes. In Fig. 5 abb 5 the slope of the characteristic curve is the internal resistance with a negative sign zero for the voltage source, infinite for the current source. In calculations, a voltage source replaces the difference of two node potentials by a known value, and a current source fixes the current of a branch. ⁠ Validity Two connections contradict the model. A short circuited voltage source would have to satisfy both and . An open current source would have to satisfy both and , because a current needs a closed path. Example. The 9 V source delivers 0.5625 A into 16 , 9 A into 1 , and it would be 9000 A into 1 m . A 0.5 A source produces 8 V across 16 , 500 V across 1 k , and it would be 500 kV across 1 M . Limiting case The more extreme the load, the further the model departs from any real device. That is the reason for the next stage. Yes. An ideal source fixes only its one quantity. If the current flows into the plus terminal of a voltage source, then , and the source absorbs power. That is how a rechargeable battery is charged. The current stays. b Nothing changes at the first resistor the current is fixed, the voltage stays 2 V. The source must produce 4 V. In series with an ideal current source, a resistor is invisible from outside. c Nothing changes at the load; it stays at 5 V and 5 mA. The source delivers 505 mA instead of 5 mA. In parallel with an ideal voltage source, a resistor is invisible from outside.

In a battery, chemistry drives charge and supplies a fixed energy per coulomb for this, the source voltage. But the current has to pass through the battery itself ions migrate through the electrolyte solution, electrons through electrodes and connections. text: One source is often not enough. A series connection raises the voltage, a parallel connection the current. This stage works out both and names the danger. The idea. In series, the same current flows through both sources, and their terminal voltages add at every current. In parallel, the same voltage lies across both, and their currents add at every voltage. That is why you calculate the series connection in the voltage source form and the parallel connection in the current source form. Two straight lines again give a straight line, and hence again a real source. Two sources in series or in parallel, respectively, act like one For the parallel connection, in voltage source form this means ⁠ How to read it The voltage in 7.2 gl 7 2 is a weighted mean, and the source with the lower resistance counts more. Two identical sources give and in parallel, and in series. Validity Series connections of voltage sources and parallel connections of current sources are technically uncritical. Parallel voltage sources need equal voltages or sufficient internal resistance for a circulating current flows even without a load, It runs out of the stronger source and into the weaker one. Two ideal voltage sources with different voltages must not be connected in parallel, nor two ideal current sources with different currents in series the model then has no solution. Both sources have the voltage , and the node rule adds their currents . This is again the form from 5.1 reale quellen und der arbeitspunkt.html gl 5 1 . With 6.1 spannungsquelle oder stromquelle.html gl 6 1 , 7.2 gl 7 2 follows. In series, the mesh rule adds the voltages in the same way. The circulating current is the loop voltage divided by the resistance of the loop. Left, two identical batteries in parallel. Right, the characteristic curves in parallel the open circuit voltage stays and the short circuit current doubles. In series the open circuit voltage doubles and the short circuit current stays. The dots show the operating points with 16 . Example. Two batteries from the reference model. In parallel 9 V, 1 , A. Current form as a check A and S. In series 18 V, 4 , A. Into 16 the parallel connection delivers 8.47 V and 0.529 A, the series connection 14.4 V and 0.9 A Fig. 8 abb 8 . The parallel connection brings little here, because 2 is small compared with 16 . If one of the batteries is discharged to 8 V, then by 7.3 gl 7 3 a current of A circulates in the open circuit. Both terminals are at 8.5 V, also according to 7.2 gl 7 2 . Limiting case With only 10 m of internal resistance each, it would be 50 A. That is why large battery cells are connected in parallel only at equal voltage. For the circulating current vanishes. In the open circuit no, both supply 9 V. Under load a little, because the current divides between two internal resistances and only half as much drops internally. The real gain is a short circuit current twice as large and twice the amount of charge. A new rechargeable battery 12.6 V, 0.1 is connected in parallel with an old one 11.8 V, 0.3 . a How large is the circulating current? What equivalent source results? b A load draws 10 A. What voltage arises, and what does each battery deliver? c Above what load current does the old battery deliver any current at all? What happens below that? a A. V, m . Check V. b V. New A. Old A. Sum 10 A. c The old battery delivers only once V, that is, for A. Below that, current flows into it, and the new battery charges it.

text: When there are several sources at different places in the network, groups alone do not help. The superposition method splits the problem into one calculation per source. The idea. A network is determined by three kinds of equations node rule, mesh rule, Ohm's law. None of them contains a product or a square of currents and voltages, as long as is fixed. Such equations are linear. If such a system has the solution for one source and the solution for another, then is the solution when both sources act at the same time. Substitution shows this every equation adds term by term. So each source drives its own current through the network as if the other were not there, and the currents add in every branch. In a linear network with independent voltage sources and independent current sources, every branch voltage and every branch current satisfies The coefficients depend only on the resistors, not on the sources. ⁠ How to read it A source is independent if its value depends on no quantity in the network. is the voltage gain from source to the voltage , without a unit this is how many volts changes per volt of the source. It is also called the sensitivity . in is the transfer resistance the transimpedance from a current source to this voltage. Correspondingly, in S and the current gain describe the current between two nodes C and D. and stand for any voltage and any current in the network. Validity only for linear networks and only for voltages and currents. The procedure. Turn off all sources except one. An ideal voltage source with the value zero forces equal potentials at its terminals, which is what a wire does it becomes a short circuit . An ideal current source with the value zero forces the current zero, which is what a gap does it becomes open terminals . Internal resistances of real sources stay in the network. Calculate the partial effect of this one source. Usually only a voltage or current divider remains. Repeat for every source and add all the partial effects with the correct signs. text: A processor knows only bits, a loudspeaker needs a voltage. The R 2R converter translates between them. It is superposition and equivalent source in a single circuit. The idea. A digital to analog converter turns a binary number with the bits into a voltage. In Fig. 12 abb 12 each switch connects its 2 resistor either to bit 1 or to 0 V bit 0 . text: A network with four terminals has three independent currents and three independent voltages. This stage shows which condition turns these into two currents and two voltages. The idea. A four pole is a network with four terminals. The node rule Part 2 /wissen/en/elektrotechnik/1 semester/grundlagen der elektrotechnik/strom widerstand und kirchhoff/strom widerstand und kirchhoff.html holds for the whole network as for one large node One terminal current is fixed by the other three. The mesh rule likewise ties together the voltages between the terminals. Now if a two terminal element, say a source, is connected to terminals 1 and 1 , a further statement is added A two terminal element has only two connections. Every charge it gives off at one it takes back at the other. The current that enters the network at terminal 1 must return at terminal 1 . The terminal pair behaves like a single access with one current and one voltage Fig. 1 abb 1 left . At a four pole with the terminals 1, 1 , 2, 2 , let all terminal currents be counted toward the network. It always holds that A terminal pair is a port if the port condition holds. A four pole with two ports is a two port Its port quantities are , , and . ⁠ How to read it 1.1 gl 1 1 leaves three currents and three voltages free. The first equation is the node rule, the second the mesh rule around the loop . 1.2 gl 1 2 removes one current each. The voltage also drops out of the description No current flows between the ports on the outside, so no power is transferred through it. Whether a four pole becomes a two port is decided by what is connected to it If a two terminal element is connected to each terminal pair, 1.2 gl 1 2 holds automatically. A branch running outside from port to port breaks it Fig. 1 abb 1 right . The historical name four pole lives on in four pole theory . Left source, two port and load. At both ports, each current returns at the second terminal, and energy flows in the forward direction from port 1 to port 2. Right An external branch from terminal 1 to terminal 2 carries the current . Now a different current flows into 1 than out of 1 , and the terminal pairs are no longer ports. A two port is a conceptually closed unit, accessible only through its ports. Its properties are fixed by the relations between the port quantities, and these can be calculated or measured. Usually a source is connected to port 1, the input , and a load to port 2, the output . Energy then flows in the forward direction ; the opposite direction is called the reverse direction . The two port is a basic structure Controlled sources are two ports, transformers, amplifiers and transistors have three or four connections, large two ports can be built from elementary two ports , and two ports joined together form a two port again. The simplest examples are the voltage divider and the current divider Part 2 /wissen/en/elektrotechnik/1 semester/grundlagen der elektrotechnik/strom widerstand und kirchhoff/strom widerstand und kirchhoff.html . Structure and classification. If a two port has a continuous line from terminal 1 to 2 , the ground line , it is called unbalanced Fig. 2 abb 2 left . It is really a three pole, an improper four pole. Network models of transistors and amplifiers are of this kind. A two port that, like the bridge circuit, has no such line and is built as a mirror image about a center line is called balanced . By their behavior, two ports are divided into linear time invariant, time varying and nonlinear ones. This chapter deals with the linear time invariant ones. text: Four port quantities are four unknowns. This stage shows why the two port contributes exactly two equations and why they contain only four numbers. The idea. Source and load each supply one equation between the voltage and the current of their port. Two are missing, and the two port supplies them. If you specify two port quantities, say both currents, all the currents and voltages inside are fixed, and so are the other two port quantities. The specified quantities are the causes, the others the effects. If the two port is linear and contains no independent sources, superposition from Part 5 /wissen/en/elektrotechnik/1 semester/grundlagen der elektrotechnik/quellen und ersatzquellen/quellen und ersatzquellen.html applies Each effect is the sum of the part due to the first cause and the part due to the second cause, each part proportional to its cause. Two effects times two causes give four factors. A time invariant two port is completely described by two two port functions , for example If it is linear and free of independent sources, then for effects and causes ⁠ How to read it The first digit of a parameter names the effect, the second the cause. The parameters depend only on the two port, not on source or load. Four quantities can be split into two causes and two effects in six ways. The four forms of this chapter are the usual ones. Validity 2.1 gl 2 1 also holds for nonlinear two ports, then as curves. For the transistor, this describes either the behavior for DC quantities or the signal behavior for small AC quantities. A transformer with separate windings transmits only time varying quantities. 2.2 gl 2 2 requires linearity. Reference arrows. To make the signs unique, a convention is needed Fig. 3 abb 3 . In the symmetric arrow system , also called the mathematical sign convention, the passive sign convention from Part 2 /wissen/en/elektrotechnik/1 semester/grundlagen der elektrotechnik/strom widerstand und kirchhoff/strom widerstand und kirchhoff.html applies at both ports The current arrows point into the two port. In the chain arrow system , also called the technical arrow system, it applies only at the input; at the output the active sign convention applies The output current points out, toward the load. This chapter uses the mixed arrow system and always point in. Where the chain form needs the current flowing out, it writes it explicitly as . A load therefore gives a negative in normal operation. The three arrow systems. Left, symmetric Both currents point into the two port. Center, chain arrows The output current points toward the load. Right, mixed, as in this chapter stays defined as on the left, and the current to the load is called . Example. At the center point of the T two port, and meet, and their sum flows through . text: Voltage is energy per charge, current is charge per time. Their product is energy per time . In a resistor, the field accelerates the electrons, and every collision hands the energy gained to the atomic lattice. That is why all the power there turns into heat, the Joule heat , with . A source with internal resistance delivers the greatest power to the load . This is called power matching . There, the energy of each charge divides equally between source and load, and the efficiency , the fraction of the power that is used, is 50 %. A fixed voltage is provided by voltage matching load large compared with the source , a fixed current by current matching load small compared with the source . Power is energy per coulomb times coulombs per second . Energy is its time integral. In a resistor, collisions give everything to the lattice , limited by . At a resistor with a sinusoidal voltage, . text: We are looking for quantities from which all branch currents follow. This stage shows why circulating currents achieve this and why the node rule then holds by itself. The idea. Imagine a separate current in each independent mesh, running in a circle Fig. 2 abb 2 . The mechanism lies in the word circle if the current enters a node through one branch, it leaves the node through another branch of the same mesh. It brings nothing into the node. This applies to every circulating current, at every node and for every numerical value. In a branch that belongs to two meshes, both circulating currents are superimposed. Only this sum is measured. Two circular bus lines share a street. On the shared street run the buses of both lines, and every line that drives into an intersection also drives out of it again. The analogy ends with the individual an electron belongs to no mesh. Mesh currents are calculation quantities; only the branch current really flows. Node 1 with the mesh currents I and II. Left each circulating current runs through the node. Right the same situation as branch currents. flows toward the node, and flow away. The sum is zero for all values. If you place a mesh current with a freely chosen direction in each of independent meshes, the current of a branch is The node rule is then satisfied for all values of the . Conversely, every current distribution that satisfies the node rule can be represented in this way. ⁠ Node rule. In a mesh, every node is connected to exactly two branches Part 2 /wissen/en/elektrotechnik/1 semester/grundlagen der elektrotechnik/strom widerstand und kirchhoff/strom widerstand und kirchhoff.html . Its current counts once flowing in and once flowing out at the node, and the contributions cancel. ⁠ Completeness. Choose a tree. Each link branch closes exactly one mesh; let its mesh current be the current of this link branch. If you subtract all these circulating currents from the given distribution, the remainder still satisfies the node rule and is zero in all link branches. It can flow only in the tree. But the tree has an end, a node with only one tree branch. There the node rule forces the current to zero. Delete this branch and repeat. The remainder is zero everywhere. ⁠ How to read it numbers the meshes, in the examples with Roman numerals. The direction is free; a negative value means that the circulating current runs the other way around. Validity The meshes must be independent. If the network can be drawn without crossings, you choose the windows , the areas between the branches. When building up from the tree, each new link branch divides exactly one area in two, so there are exactly windows. Example. text: A program sees no meshes and rearranges nothing. This stage shows how the matrix arises component by component, without any component having to know the others. The idea. A component touches only its two nodes. Its current therefore appears in exactly two node equations, in one with plus, in the other with minus. So each component has a fixed entry pattern, its stamp Fig. 7 abb 7 . You begin with a matrix full of zeros and add the stamps component by component. The order does not matter. Entry patterns in the rows and columns of the nodes. Left conductance between and . Center fixed current source that pushes from to ; it enters only on the right hand side. Right voltage controlled current source from to . It stands in the rows , , but in the columns , Stage 8 gesteuerte quellen und verstarker.html stufe 8 . Each row is the node rule “outgoing currents = impressed currents”. A conductance between and carries the current from to . It adds to the positions and and to and . A fixed current source that pushes through itself from to adds in row and in row of the right hand side. It enters nothing in , because its current depends on no voltage. ⁠ How to read it First, each of the nodes gets a row and a column, including the reference node. This full matrix has determinant zero, because all rows have the sum zero if you raise all potentials together, no additional current flows anywhere. Physically, a network determines only differences. Only fixing makes the solution unique you delete column 0 because its unknown is zero, and row 0 because it follows from the other node rules Part 2 /wissen/en/elektrotechnik/1 semester/grundlagen der elektrotechnik/strom widerstand und kirchhoff/strom widerstand und kirchhoff.html . What remains is from Stage 5 das knotenpotentialverfahren.html stufe 5 . Validity The stamps apply to linear components. Voltage sources follow in Stage 9 die modifizierte knotenanalyse.html stufe 9 . Netlist. A circuit diagram is stored as a netlist one line per component, consisting of name, nodes and value. In SPICE, R3 1 2 2k means resistor between the nodes 1 and 2. I2 0 2 4m means 4 mA through the source from node 0 to node 2. The program goes through the list line by line and stamps. If a new node name appears, the matrix grows by one row and one column. Nobody has to know its size beforehand. The rigid format dates from the 1970s, when SPICE was written in FORTRAN and each line occupied a punched card. Example. The model network with the converted battery gives this list | Line | Value | Entry | | | | | | R1 1 0 1k | | at , ; at , | | R2 1 0 4k | | at , ; at , | | R3 1 2 2k | | at , ; at , | | R4 2 0 10k | | at , ; at , | | R5 2 0 5k | | at , ; at , | | I1 0 1 9m | | right in row 1, in row 0 | | I2 0 2 4m | | right in row 2, in row 0 | With the rows and columns in the order 0, 1, 2 this gives Each row sums to zero. If you delete row and column 0, the system from Stage 5 das knotenpotentialverfahren.html stufe 5 remains. Check In the reduced , the row sum is the conductance to ground and . Limiting case A node without a branch to ground has the row sum zero. Large networks. A node is usually connected to only two to five neighbors, so almost all positions of a large matrix are zero. It is called sparse . The simulator stores only the nonzero entries and solves the system by stepwise elimination. Cramer's rule would be useless for this a determinant with 20 rows has around products following the pattern of 0.1 von grund auf drei gleichungen drei unbekannte.html gl 0 1 . With sinusoidal quantities you calculate with complex conductances, the admittances. That is where the letters and come from. A capacitor has the same stamp as a conductance. An impedance can be entered only as as long as it is not zero; a coil at frequency zero breaks this. Stage 9 die modifizierte knotenanalyse.html stufe 9 solves this problem. The simulator replaces nonlinear components such as diodes Part 9 /wissen/en/elektrotechnik/1 semester/grundlagen der elektrotechnik/halbleiter und dioden/halbleiter und dioden.html by the tangent of their characteristic curve, stamps it and repeats this until nothing changes any more. Each of the node equations follows from the others Part 2 /wissen/en/elektrotechnik/1 semester/grundlagen der elektrotechnik/strom widerstand und kirchhoff/strom widerstand und kirchhoff.html . You could delete any of them. You delete the row of the reference node because, together with its column, a symmetric matrix results again and because the current into ground is rarely of interest. The list R1 1 0 1k , R2 1 2 2k , R3 2 0 2k , I1 0 1 7m , I2 2 1 1m is given. Stamp the full matrix and the right hand side. Check the row sums. Delete the reference node and solve. All row sums are zero, and the sum on the right is zero too. b with , , . So V, V. c Through R1 flow 6 mA into ground, through R3 1 mA, together 7 mA. I1 takes exactly 7 mA out of ground.

text: What this is about A charger turns the AC voltage of the wall outlet into the DC voltage for the rechargeable battery. The component that does this is called a diode it lets current through in one direction forward direction and blocks it in the other reverse direction . It consists of a semiconductor , a material whose conductivity lies between that of a metal and that of an insulator and can be set deliberately. The question of this chapter is How does a piece of silicon become a valve for current, and how do you calculate with a component that does not obey Ohm's law? The answer runs through six terms. Doping means building in a few foreign atoms, which fixes how many charge carriers mobile charges the crystal has. At the boundary between two differently doped regions, the pn junction , the space charge region forms by itself, a thin layer without mobile charges that acts as an energy barrier. The characteristic curve is the graph of current versus voltage, the operating point the pair of voltage and current that settles in a circuit. How to work with this chapter. In a single atom, electrons have only certain energies, the energy levels . In a crystal regular lattice of atoms the shells overlap, and the electrons belong to the whole crystal. No two electrons may occupy the same state. That is why each level splits into as many closely spaced levels as the crystal has atoms. This creates a band of allowed energies. The conduction band CB lies above it and is empty at . The band gap is the smallest energy that lifts an electron from the VB into the CB. The Fermi energy separates occupied from empty states at . text: An n piece and a p piece are, on their own, just resistors. This stage shows what forms at their boundary and why it is a barrier. The idea. In a crystal, a p region borders an n region. Four steps take place Fig. 4 abb 4 ⁠ Diffusion. Charge carriers move randomly. More of them wander out of the region of high density than into it. This equalization by random motion is called diffusion . Electrons wander from the n region into the p region, holes the other way. ⁠ Recombination. In the foreign region the wanderers meet the majority there and disappear. Near the boundary, hardly any free carriers remain afterward. ⁠ Fixed ions remain. There the ions are no longer balanced on the n side, on the p side. This stationary charge is called space charge , the layer the space charge region. ⁠ The field stops the equalization. text: At the pn junction, mobile charges move into the other region and leave fixed ions behind. The field of these ions builds up a barrier in the space charge region that stops the equalization. Heat lifts only the fraction of the charge carriers over a barrier of height . Voltage in the forward direction lowers the barrier, so the current grows exponentially, by a factor of 10 per 60 mV . In the reverse direction only the tiny current remains. In a circuit, the operating point lies at the intersection of the characteristic curve and the load line the straight line set by source and resistor . For hand calculations the diode becomes a switch with a fixed forward voltage, and for small changes around the operating point it becomes a resistor . ft_text: how a small voltage controls a large current through a blocking diode in n doped silicon, electrons are free to move; in p doped silicon, holes are missing electrons that move like positive charges. at the boundary between the two regions, the pn junction , the space charge region forms a strip with almost no free carriers, in which fixed ions produce an electric field from the n region to the p region. this field acts as a barrier for the majority carriers of each side. plus at the p region lowers it, and the diode conducts in the forward direction . plus at the n region raises it, and the diode blocks. diffusion is the motion of particles from a dense place to a sparse one; recombination is the encounter of an electron with a hole, in which both disappear as free carriers. for the diode follows the equation , and at the operating point one calculates with the tangent to its characteristic curve.
text: In n doped silicon, electrons are free to move; in p doped silicon, holes are missing electrons that move like positive charges. At the boundary between the two regions, the pn junction , the space charge region forms a strip with almost no free carriers, in which fixed ions produce an electric field from the n region to the p region. This field acts as a barrier for the majority carriers of each side. Plus at the p region lowers it, and the diode conducts in the forward direction . Plus at the n region raises it, and the diode blocks. Diffusion is the motion of particles from a dense place to a sparse one; recombination is the encounter of an electron with a hole, in which both disappear as free carriers. For the diode follows the equation , and at the operating point one calculates with the tangent to its characteristic curve.

An npn transistor consists of three regions of the same semiconductor n doped emitter, p doped base, n doped collector Fig. 1 abb 1 . text: The CB diode blocks, and yet milliamperes flow through it. This stage follows the path of the electrons and shows why only a small base current is needed. The idea. A blocking diode does not block because its boundary is impermeable. It blocks because almost no free electrons are available on the p side. The field of the space charge region drives every electron that reaches the boundary from the p side across into the n region. For such electrons the boundary is a steep drop Fig. 2 abb 2 , bottom . The transistor supplies exactly these missing electrons, in four steps ⁠ Injection. lowers the barrier at the BE boundary. Electrons from the emitter enter the base. This introduction is called injection . The electron density at the emitter edge of the base grows with . ⁠ Crossing. In the p type base, electrons are a minority among many holes. They diffuse to the collector edge, where their density is almost zero. The base is much narrower than the diffusion length , the mean distance until recombination, several tens of µ m. That is why almost all of them get through. ⁠ Sweeping out. At the collector edge, the field of the CB boundary catches every arriving electron and pulls it into the collector. How large is hardly matters; the field always collects them all. That is why hardly depends on . ⁠ Replenishing. Two small losses remain holes from the base pass into the emitter, and some electrons recombine in the base. Both use up holes. The base terminal must replace them. This replacement is the base current. It stays small because the emitter is much more heavily doped than the base and because the base is so narrow. text: With exponential functions, circuits can hardly be solved by hand. This stage replaces the surface with three linear pieces. The idea. Each of the two diodes can conduct or block. This gives the operating states. If the BE diode blocks, no electron starts and nothing flows. This is the cut off region . If it conducts and the CB diode blocks, the collector collects all the electrons, and holds. This is the active region. If falls so far that the CB diode conducts noticeably as well, the collector sends electrons back. Then it can no longer collect them all, the base fills up with electrons, and stays below . This is the saturation region . text: What this is about An operational amplifier , op amp for short, is an integrated amplifier made of a few dozen transistors. It amplifies the voltage between its two inputs by a factor of about 100000. This factor is called the open loop gain . It varies by a factor of four from one specimen to the next and changes with temperature. Nevertheless, this component is used to build amplifiers that feel only 0.01 % of this variation, as well as summing amplifiers and integrators. The question is How does a huge, imprecise factor turn into a component whose behavior is determined by the resistors alone? The answer is negative feedback part of the output voltage is fed back to the input in such a way that it counteracts its own cause. How to work with this chapter. text: A sensor delivers millivolts, and every conductor produces a random interference voltage. This stage clarifies where it comes from, how it is measured, and what an amplifier can do about it. The idea. Noise is a disturbance made up of many oscillations of different frequency and amplitude. Its waveform is random and can only be described statistically the mean is zero, and the rms value measures its strength. Because independent disturbances sometimes reinforce and sometimes cancel each other, it is not their rms values that add but the squares of these values. That is why noise is described by the noise voltage density the contribution of each frequency strip 1 Hz wide to the square of the rms value. The rms value of the noise voltage and the density of the thermal noise of a resistor are The signal to noise ratio is the ratio of the powers, written in decibels dB ⁠ How to read it . J/K is the Boltzmann constant it converts temperature into mean thermal energy per particle. is the absolute temperature in K, the resistance. is the base 10 logarithm. 20 dB mean a factor of 10 in voltage and 100 in power. Validity The right hand part of 1.1 gl 1 1 holds up to far beyond the frequencies of electronics. | Type | Mechanism | Density | | | | | | Thermal noise | Thermal motion of the charge carriers in every conductor. Random accumulations at the ends produce a voltage, even without current flow. | constant, | | Shot noise | Current consists of individual charges that cross a potential barrier at random times, for example in the pn junction. | constant | | 1/f noise | Recharging of surface states, fluctuating number of free charge carriers in the semiconductor. | , interferes up to about 10 kHz | Constant density is called white noise , after white light made of all colors. This is a shape of the spectrum, not a cause. Integrated over all frequencies it would give infinite power. The sensor resistor has , so in 20 kHz, µ V. The useful signal of 1 mV is 549 times larger dB. Half the bandwidth lowers the noise by , which is 3 dB. Limiting cases For or the thermal noise vanishes. What an amplifier changes. It raises the signal and the noise present at its input by the same factor, so the SNR stays the same or gets worse through the amplifier's own noise. It helps only against disturbances that join in behind it and have a fixed size. If the line to the next device adds 100 µ V, then 20.0 dB remain without an amplifier. With a gain of 100 at the sensor it is , that is, 53.7 dB. The second remedy is the difference a disturbance that hits two lines equally vanishes if only their difference is evaluated. text: The amplifier stages become a component with a few terminals. This stage fixes its model and shows what it does without an external circuit it compares. The idea. The op amp has two inputs, one output and two terminals for the supply, and Fig. 3 abb 3 . It has no ground terminal the output refers to the middle of the supply. Every output current comes from the supply terminals, which are usually omitted in circuit diagrams. That is why the three visible terminals do not satisfy the node rule. The output delivers times , but only up to its limits. With V and the linear portion already ends at µ V. Any larger difference drives the output to a limit, saturation . The question of this chapter is What exactly must be assumed about numbers so that all the rules of arithmetic become provable, and what distinguishes the real numbers from the fractions? The answer needs two tools and a short list of assumptions. A set collects objects; a statement is a sentence that is true or false. An axiom is a basic assumption that is laid down and not proved. Three groups of axioms suffice A field is a set in which plus and times work according to the familiar rules. The order fixes which numbers are positive. Completeness says that the number line has no gaps. In addition there are mathematical induction , the proof method for statements about all natural numbers, and the absolute value , the distance of a number from zero. How to work with this chapter. text: What this is about A temperature sensor delivers exactly one voltage for each temperature. Such an assignment is called a function Every input gets exactly one output . Going forward, substituting is enough. What is usually needed is the way back For the measured voltage we seek the temperature , that is, the solution of the equation . The question of this chapter is When does have exactly one solution, and how do you find the solutions of for the most important functions, the polynomials? The answer leads through seven concepts. The inverse function provides the way back as a function in its own right. A polynomial is a sum of powers of with fixed numbers in front. A zero is an with ; it comes with a linear factor , a factor of degree one. The Horner scheme is the computational procedure that splits it off. Then there are the rational function , a quotient of two polynomials, and the pole , where its denominator becomes zero and its absolute value grows beyond every bound. How to work with this chapter. A system is called linear if the superposition principle holds for arbitrary constants time invariant if for every shift A linear, time invariant system is called an LTI system for short LTI stands for linear time invariant . Time invariance comes from the fact that and do not change with time. Every network of , and is described by linear differential equations with constant coefficients. This stage shows that this works, what the weights are called and where the limits lie. Starting point pure oscillations On the imaginary axis the building blocks are pure oscillations . An absolutely integrable signal , so it decays fast enough on both sides can be built from them. This is the Fourier representation . Its formula is all that is needed here. The function is called the spectrum ; it gives the weight of the oscillation with frequency For many signals in system theory this is not enough. The step does not decay, and the impulse response of an unstable system even grows. A signal that grows without bound cannot be built from oscillations of constant amplitude.

text: What kinds of signals are there, and how is sampling described mathematically? Four classes. Time and amplitude can each be continuous or discrete. An analog signal is continuous in both. A discrete time signal has values only at the times , but these with arbitrary precision. A digital signal is in addition stepped in amplitude quantized , because a computer can represent only finitely many numbers. This chapter deals with the discretization of time. The quantization of the amplitude is a separate topic. From the real to the ideal sampler. In every clock cycle, a real sampler closes a switch for the short time If is made shorter and shorter, only the values remain. Mathematically, the rectangle is replaced by a Dirac impulse. This is the ideal sampler The sampled signal is a train of Dirac impulses, each with a sample as its weight. The second step is the sifting property . In this form, sampled signals can be treated with all the tools for continuous signals.

text: How do you describe a signal whose waveform you do not know? You imagine many signals of the same kind and average over them. The idea. If you measure the noise of many identically built resistors at the same temperature, you get many different curves , Fig. 1 abb 1 . Each one is called a sample function or realization. The imagined totality of all of them is called a random process . The values of all sample functions at a fixed instant form a random variable . ⁠ How to read it is called the expected value or ensemble average you average over all sample functions at the same instant, that is, vertically in Fig. 1 abb 1 . With you obtain the mean square value. The autocorrelation function averages the product of the values at two instants. It tells you how strongly the value at is related to the value at . Three sample functions of a random process simulated, mean value 1 . The ensemble average is formed vertically, over all sample functions at the same red, dashed . The time average is formed horizontally, along one sample function.

text: So far, lines were ideal connections. If a line is long compared with the wavelength, a signal needs a noticeable time to travel through it. This stage sets up the equations that describe this. The idea. The line is divided into short pieces of length . Each piece has a series resistance and a series inductance the outgoing and return conductors , plus a shunt capacitance and a shunt conductance between the conductors . For a uniform line these quantities are proportional to the length , , , , with the per unit length parameters line constants , , , values per meter, Fig. 1 abb 1 .
